mentions.quote: Having honored Yājñavalkya, the lord of yogis, the sages spoke
mentions.role: protagonist and authority

mentions.quote: Residing in Mithilā, that king of yogis, having meditated for a moment, said to the sages
mentions.role: speaker and lawgiver

mentions.quote: Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: The sage Yājñavalkya, the central authority of this dharmaśāstra text, who teaches the assembled sages on dharma from Mithilā.
entities.justification: Yājñavalkya is the text's primary speaker and namesake, honored by the sages and described as 'lord of yogis' who expounds dharma.

mentions.quote: Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: Manu, the primordial lawgiver, listed as one of the authoritative promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras.
entities.justification: Manu is explicitly named among the recognized sages whose teachings constitute the body of dharmaśāstra authority.

mentions.quote: Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: Vyāsa, the sage traditionally credited with compiling the Vedas and authoring the Mahābhārata, named among dharmaśāstra authorities.
entities.justification: Vyāsa is explicitly listed alongside other sages as a promulgator of the Dharmaśāstras in the opening enumeration of authorities.

mentions.quote: Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: Bṛhaspati, preceptor of the gods and recognized dharmaśāstra authority, named in the canonical list of lawgivers.
entities.justification: Bṛhaspati is explicitly enumerated among the dharmaśāstra promulgators in the text's opening canonical list.

mentions.quote: Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: Parāśara, a Vedic sage and father of Vyāsa, listed as one of the recognized promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras.
entities.justification: Parāśara is explicitly named in the canonical enumeration of dharmaśāstra authorities at the text's opening.

mentions.quote: Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: Vasiṣṭha, one of the seven great sages (saptarṣis), explicitly named as a promulgator of the Dharmaśāstras.
entities.justification: Vasiṣṭha is the last-named figure in the canonical list of dharmaśāstra authorities, closing the enumeration.

mentions.quote: Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati
mentions.role: listed as a promulgator of dharmaśāstra

entities.description: Yama, the god of death and dharmic justice, included among the recognized promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras.
entities.justification: Yama is explicitly enumerated in the canonical list of dharmaśāstra authorities, occupying a position between sages.

mentions.quote: The base of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, and the tip of the hand, are the Prajāpati, Pitṛ, Brahma, and Deva tīrthas, respectively
mentions.role: deity associated with a ritual water-pouring point on the hand

entities.description: Prajāpati, the lord of creatures and primordial creator deity, whose sacred tīrtha is identified with the base of the little finger.
entities.justification: Prajāpati is identified as the deity of a specific tīrtha (sacred point) on the hand used in ritual water-sipping.

mentions.quote: The base of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb, and the tip of the hand, are the Prajāpati, Pitṛ, Brahma, and Deva tīrthas
mentions.role: deity associated with a ritual tīrtha on the thumb

mentions.quote: he attains the world of Brahma and is not born here again
mentions.role: lord of the highest world attainable by a perpetual celibate

mentions.quote: Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas
mentions.role: creator of the Brāhmaṇa varna

mentions.quote: the gift of Brahman (sacred knowledge) comprises all dharmas and is superior to all other gifts, one who gives it attains the eternal world of Brahma
mentions.role: lord of the eternal world attained through giving sacred knowledge

entities.description: Brahmā, the creator deity, who created the Brāhmaṇas through austerities, is associated with the highest cosmic world attained through celibacy and sacred knowledge.
entities.justification: Brahmā appears in multiple roles: as a ritual tīrtha, as the creator of Brāhmaṇas, and as the lord of the highest world attained through spiritual practice.

mentions.quote: Soma gave them purity, Gandharva gave them sweet speech
mentions.role: deity who granted purity to women

entities.description: Soma, the moon-deity and lord of the sacred drink, credited with granting purity to women in a mythological enumeration.
entities.justification: Soma is named as a deity who bestowed a divine gift (purity) upon women, establishing their sacred nature.

mentions.quote: Gandharva gave them sweet speech
mentions.role: deity who granted sweet speech to women

entities.description: Gandharva, the celestial musician, credited with bestowing sweet speech upon women in the mythological passage on their divine gifts.
entities.justification: Gandharva is named as the source of women's sweet speech in a theological justification for women's purity.

mentions.quote: Pāvaka (Fire) gave them all-purifying nature; therefore, women are indeed pure
mentions.role: deity who granted all-purifying nature to women

entities.description: Pāvaka (Fire), the purifying deity, credited with granting women their all-purifying nature as a divine gift.
entities.justification: Pāvaka is named as the divine source of women's purifying quality, forming part of the theological argument for women's inherent purity.

mentions.quote: She who does not go to another man, whether her husband is alive or dead, attains fame in this world and rejoices with Umā in the next
mentions.role: divine companion awarded to a chaste wife in the afterlife

entities.description: Umā, the consort of Śiva and goddess of devotion, cited as the heavenly companion with whom a faithful wife is reunited in the afterlife.
entities.justification: Umā appears as the eschatological reward for wifely fidelity, marking the highest feminine spiritual attainment.

mentions.quote: Residing in Mithilā, that king of yogis, having meditated for a moment, said to the sages
mentions.role: location where Yājñavalkya delivers his teaching

entities.description: Mithilā, the ancient city and capital of the Videha kingdom, identified as the location where Yājñavalkya resides and gives his teachings.
entities.justification: Mithilā is given as the specific geographical setting of the text's framing dialogue, grounding the teaching in a real sacred site.

mentions.quote: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are the varṇas; the first three are the twice-born
mentions.role: first and highest varṇa

mentions.quote: Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas
mentions.role: divinely created class charged with preserving the Vedas

mentions.quote: For a Brāhmaṇa, accepting gifts, sacrificing for others, and teaching are additional
mentions.role: class with distinctive duties

entities.description: The Brāhmaṇa, the priestly and scholarly varṇa created by Brahmā to protect the Vedas, with special duties of teaching, sacrificing for others, and accepting gifts.
entities.justification: Brāhmaṇas are the most extensively discussed social group in this window, with their creation, privileges, duties, and ritual status elaborated throughout.

mentions.quote: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are the varṇas; the first three are the twice-born
mentions.role: second varṇa

mentions.quote: The primary duty for a Kṣatriya is the protection of the people
mentions.role: warrior class with duty to protect

entities.description: The Kṣatriya, the warrior and ruling varṇa, whose primary duty is the protection of the people, alongside sacrificing, studying, and giving.
entities.justification: The Kṣatriya class is repeatedly defined by its protective duty and occupies distinct positions in the varna hierarchy throughout the text.

mentions.quote: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are the varṇas; the first three are the twice-born
mentions.role: third varṇa

mentions.quote: Money-lending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing are prescribed for a Vaiśya
mentions.role: mercantile class with economic duties

entities.description: The Vaiśya, the mercantile and agricultural varṇa, whose prescribed occupations include money-lending, agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
entities.justification: The Vaiśya is defined by its economic functions and twice-born status, appearing in multiple contexts of duty assignment and social ordering.

mentions.quote: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are the varṇas; the first three are the twice-born
mentions.role: fourth and lowest varṇa, not twice-born

mentions.quote: The duty of a Śūdra is the service of the twice-born; if unable to live by that, he may become a merchant
mentions.role: servile class with duty of service

entities.description: The Śūdra, the fourth and lowest varṇa, excluded from the twice-born initiation, whose prescribed duty is service to the three higher varṇas.
entities.justification: The Śūdra is consistently defined by its subordinate position and service duty, contrasted with the privileges of the twice-born throughout the text.

mentions.quote: from a Śūdra is born a Caṇḍāla, who is excluded from all dharma
mentions.role: outcaste group born of highest-lowest hypergamy

mentions.quote: He should place food on the ground for dogs, Caṇḍālas, and crows
mentions.role: recipients of the Bali offering placed on the ground

mentions.quote: One becomes a Caṇḍāla by performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra
mentions.role: paradigmatic state of ritual degradation

entities.description: The Caṇḍāla, the most degraded social group born of the union of a Śūdra man and a Brāhmaṇa woman (pratiloma), excluded from all dharma and recipients only of ground-level food offerings.
entities.justification: Caṇḍālas appear as the limit-case of social exclusion: excluded from dharma, fed along with dogs and crows, and used as the paradigm of ritual degradation.

mentions.quote: the twice-born who studies the Ṛg-Veda daily gratifies the gods, and the Ancestors with honey and ghee
mentions.role: sacred text whose daily recitation gratifies gods and ancestors

entities.description: The Ṛg-Veda, the oldest of the four Vedas, whose daily study by the twice-born generates cosmic merit that gratifies both gods and the ancestors.
entities.justification: The Ṛg-Veda is individually named with its specific ritual effects, affirming its role as a primary source of cosmic merit through recitation.

mentions.quote: He who daily studies the Yajur-Veda according to his ability gratifies the gods with libations of ghee and nectar
mentions.role: sacred text whose daily study gratifies gods with ghee and nectar

entities.description: The Yajur-Veda, the ritual Veda of sacrificial formulae, whose daily study is said to gratify the gods with ghee and nectar and the ancestors similarly.
entities.justification: The Yajur-Veda is named with its specific meritorious effects, establishing each Veda's distinct ritual potency.

mentions.quote: He who daily recites the Sāma-Veda gratifies the gods with Soma and ghee
mentions.role: sacred text whose recitation gratifies gods with Soma and ghee

entities.description: The Sāma-Veda, the Veda of melodies and chants, whose daily recitation gratifies the gods with Soma and ghee.
entities.justification: The Sāma-Veda is listed with its own distinctive cosmic reward, paralleling the effects of the other Vedas.

mentions.quote: Reciting the Atharvāṅgirasa, the twice-born gratifies the gods with fat
mentions.role: sacred text whose recitation generates merit for gods and ancestors

entities.description: The Atharva-Veda (Atharvāṅgirasa), the fourth Veda dealing with spells and household rites, whose daily recitation gratifies gods with fat and ancestors with honey.
entities.justification: The Atharvāṅgirasa is named as the fourth of the canonical Vedas with its own distinctive meritorious effects.

mentions.quote: One should repeat the Gāyatrī, together with the Śiras, preceded by the Vyahṛtis, and joined with Praṇava at the beginning and end
mentions.role: sacred mantra to be repeated at twilight worship

entities.description: The Gāyatrī, the most sacred Vedic mantra (Ṛg-Veda 3.62.10), to be recited with specific prefixes and suffixes during the twilight worship ritual.
entities.justification: The Gāyatrī is specified as the central mantra of the twice-born's daily twilight worship practice.

themes.topic: Dharma as cosmic and social order

mentions.quote: Declare to us in their entirety the dharma of the varṇas, the life-stages, and the others
Revelation (the Vedas), tradition (the Smṛtis), the conduct of the virtuous, what is pleasing to one's own self, and desire born of right resolve—this is declared to be the root of dharma
Of sacrifice, right conduct, sense-control, non-violence, giving, and the study of the Veda—of these actions, this is the highest dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga

themes.justification: Dharma is the organizing concept of the entire window: its sources, hierarchy, and culmination in yogic self-knowledge are laid out at the outset and govern every subsequent prescription.

themes.topic: Authority and canonicity of sacred knowledge (Veda, Smṛti, Dharmaśāstra)

mentions.quote: The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the Aṅgas, together with the Vedas, are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of dharma
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras, Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama, Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras

themes.justification: The text immediately establishes its epistemic foundation by enumerating fourteen sources of dharmic knowledge and twenty named sages whose texts constitute the tradition's canon.

themes.topic: Varṇāśrama dharma: duties of the four social orders and four life-stages

mentions.quote: Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra are the varṇas; the first three are the twice-born
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are the duties of a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya. For a Brāhmaṇa, accepting gifts, sacrificing for others, and teaching are additional
The primary duty for a Kṣatriya is the protection of the people

themes.justification: The bulk of the window systematically prescribes specific duties for each varṇa and each āśrama (student, householder, graduate), which is the text's central organizing structure.

mentions.quote: Holding his generative organ, he should rise and, with earth and water drawn for the purpose, diligently perform the purification of the lower body
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, throat, and palate, respectively, according to their number
Bathing with mantras sacred to the water deities, purification by sprinkling, and control of the breath

themes.justification: The student conduct section and the entire chapter 8 on purification of things demonstrate that ritual purity is a pervasive structuring concern governing bodies, objects, substances, and spaces.

themes.topic: Brahmacarya (student celibacy) and the transmission of Vedic knowledge

mentions.quote: 2. The Student Celibate (brahmacāriprakaraṇam)
He is a Guru who, having performed the rites, bestows the Veda upon him. He who initiates and imparts the Veda is called an Ācārya
Mortifying his body by this rule, with his senses conquered, he attains the world of Brahma and is not born here again

themes.justification: An entire section (chapter 2) is devoted to the brahmacarī's vows, practices, and teachers, presenting celibate studentship as the foundational life-stage for the twice-born.

themes.topic: Marriage forms and the regulation of sexual and reproductive life

mentions.quote: 3. Marriage (vivāhaprakaraṇam)
The Brāhma marriage is when a maiden, adorned according to one's ability, is given after being invited; a son born of it purifies twenty-one generations on both sides
The Āsura marriage is from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, by mutual agreement; the Rākṣasa, by capture in battle; the Paiśāca, by the deceitful seduction of a maiden

themes.justification: Section 3 elaborates eight forms of marriage ranked by purity and soteriological efficacy, establishing marriage as a central mechanism of social reproduction and ritual status.

themes.topic: Status of women, wifely duty, and female purity

mentions.quote: Soma gave them purity, Gandharva gave them sweet speech, and Pāvaka (Fire) gave them all-purifying nature; therefore, women are indeed pure
A wife must carry out her husband's word; this is the highest dharma for a woman
She who does not go to another man, whether her husband is alive or dead, attains fame in this world and rejoices with Umā in the next

themes.justification: Multiple verses address women's inherent purity (through divine gifts), their prescribed duties of fidelity and obedience, and their heavenly rewards, constituting a sustained theology of femininity.

themes.topic: Varna mixture and the classification of mixed-caste groups

mentions.quote: 4. The Distinction of Castes and Births (varṇajātivivekaprakaraṇam)
From a Brāhmaṇa on a Kṣatriya woman, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born; on a Vaiśya woman, an Ambaṣṭha; on a Śūdra woman, a Niṣāda is born
An elevation of caste is known to occur in the seventh or even the fifth generation in an age

themes.justification: Section 4 is entirely devoted to the genealogical classification of offspring from inter-varna unions, systematically cataloguing pratiloma and anuloma categories.

themes.topic: The five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) as the householder's cosmic duties

mentions.quote: The offering to all beings, the oblation to the Ancestors, the oblation to the gods, Vedic study, and hospitality to guests—these are the great sacrifices (mahāyajñas) to the beings, Ancestors, gods, Brahman, and men
From the food remaining after the oblation to the gods, he should offer the Bali offering to all beings. He should place food on the ground for dogs, Caṇḍālas, and crows
he should not neglect the five great sacrifices, using the mantra of salutation

themes.justification: The text explicitly names and mandates the five great sacrifices as the non-negotiable daily duties of the householder, integrating cosmic obligation into domestic life.

themes.topic: Gift-giving (dāna) as meritorious and soteriological action

mentions.quote: Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the Ancestors and gods, and for the preservation of dharma
The giver of such a cow attains heaven for as many years as there are hairs on its body
Because the gift of Brahman (sacred knowledge) comprises all dharmas and is superior to all other gifts, one who gives it attains the eternal world of Brahma

themes.justification: Section 9 (Dānaprakaraṇam) dedicates a full chapter to the mechanics and rewards of gift-giving, ranking gifts by their soteriological power and identifying sacred knowledge as the supreme gift.

themes.topic: Dietary rules: edible and inedible substances

mentions.quote: 7. Edible and Inedible Foods (bhakṣyābhakṣyaprakaraṇam)
Among five-toed animals, the iguana, tortoise, and porcupine are edible; also the hare, and among fish, the Siṃhatuṇḍa and Rohita
In peril of life, at a śrāddha, when it has been consecrated, or at the request of a Brāhmaṇa, one who eats meat after having worshipped the gods and the Ancestors is not tainted by meat

themes.justification: Section 7 codifies an extensive taxonomy of permitted and forbidden foods, animals, and their exceptions, demonstrating that dietary regulation is a major axis of the text's purity code.

themes.topic: Yoga and self-knowledge as the highest spiritual attainment

mentions.quote: Of sacrifice, right conduct, sense-control, non-violence, giving, and the study of the Veda—of these actions, this is the highest dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga
Mortifying his body by this rule, with his senses conquered, he attains the world of Brahma and is not born here again
Having honored Yājñavalkya, the lord of yogis

themes.justification: Although presented in a legal-ritual text, Yājñavalkya's opening verse places yoga and Self-knowledge above all ritual actions, and his title 'lord of yogis' signals an implicit Vedāntic soteriology underlying the dharmaśāstra framework.

citations.quote: Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, Aṅgiras
citations.justification: Manu is named as the first in a canonical list of dharmaśāstra authorities, implicitly invoking his text as a co-source of dharmic norms alongside the present work.

citations.quote: Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati
citations.justification: Āpastamba is named as a recognized authority in the canonical list of dharmaśāstra promulgators, placing his work within the tradition the present text claims to continue.

citations.quote: Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras
citations.justification: Vasiṣṭha is named as one of the twenty authoritative dharmaśāstra promulgators whose teachings the present work situates itself within and extends.

citations.quote: Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama
citations.justification: Vyāsa is included among the canonical dharmaśāstra authorities, invoking his textual tradition as part of the recognized body of dharmic sources.

citations.quote: Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, and Gautama
citations.justification: Parāśara's dharmaśāstra is implicitly cited by naming him in the canonical list of authoritative promulgators the present text acknowledges.

citations.quote: The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the Aṅgas, together with the Vedas, are the fourteen sources of knowledge and of dharma
citations.justification: The Purāṇas are included among the fourteen authoritative sources of dharma, constituting a generic citation of the purāṇic textual corpus as a co-source of sacred knowledge.
